Contributions to the Study of SMS Spam Filtering: New Collection and Results
Tiago A. Almeida; José María Gómez Hidalgo; Akebo Yamakami
Proc. 11th ACM Symposium on Document Engineering (DocEng '11), Mountain View, CA, USA, 19-22 Sep 2011, pp. 259-262

Release a public, real, non-encoded SMS spam corpus and report baseline results of established classifiers on it. Motivation: few public SMS corpora, few features per message, and idiom/abbreviation-heavy text.
SMS Spam Collection v.1, assembled from Grumbletext (425 spam), NUS SMS Corpus (3,375 ham), C. Tagg thesis (450 ham) and SMS Spam Corpus v.0.1 Big (1,002 ham, 322 spam).
5,574 messages: 4,827 ham (86.60%) and 747 spam (13.40%); 81,175 tokens in total.
English; Latin script; raw text.
ham, spam

14 classifier entries (several naive Bayes variants, boosted NB, linear SVM, MDL, kNN with K=1/3/5, C4.5, boosted C4.5, PART) with two tokenizers (tok1, tok2); WEKA defaults; no stop-word removal, stemming or dimensionality reduction. EM clustering and a trivial rejector are used as baselines. Near-duplicate check uses N-gram string matching.

[Reported] Linear SVM + tok1 was best by MCC: spam caught 83.10%, blocked ham 0.18%, accuracy 97.64%, MCC 0.893. Boosted NB, boosted C4.5 and PART reached 97.50% accuracy (MCC 0.887); the authors state the best four were not statistically different. Trivial rejector accuracy 86.95%. Authors conclude SVM is a good baseline.
Spam caught (SC%), blocked ham (BH%), accuracy, Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC).
Public and real messages; transparent protocol; duplicate analysis reported; ham-blocking rate reported separately from accuracy.

[Authors] Limited public data, few features per message, idioms and abbreviations. [Our reading] One fixed split (first 30% train, remaining 70% test), no cross-validation or variance; spam and ham come largely from different sources, so source may correlate with label; English only; the task is unsolicited-spam filtering, not phishing; the text read does not describe TF-IDF weighting.

FOUNDATIONAL baseline. Supports a linear SVM as a strong, simple short-text baseline and the habit of reporting ham-blocking rate. It does not validate TF-IDF specifically and says nothing about phishing, Malayalam or Manglish.
No Malayalam, Manglish or code-mixed counterpart; no phishing labels; single-split evaluation.

A. Baseline paper (Almeida et al., 2011): how it supports our SVM baseline, and its limits
Topic
Finding
Basis
What it reports

A public English SMS corpus (5,574 messages, 13.40% spam) and a comparison of 14 classifier entries. Linear SVM + tok1 was best by MCC (0.893), catching 83.10% of spam and blocking 0.18% of ham, with 97.64% accuracy. The best four classifiers were not statistically different.
[Reported] P01 Tables 1-4
How it supports TF-IDF + linear SVM
It supports a linear SVM as a strong, simple baseline on short messages with sparse token features and no dimensionality reduction, and it models the habit of reporting blocked ham next to accuracy.
[Reported] P01 Section 3
What it does not support

It does not describe TF-IDF weighting in the text read (it uses two tokenizers and WEKA defaults). The choice of TF-IDF, and of word vs character n-grams for Malayalam and Manglish, is our design decision and should be justified with an ablation.
[Our reading]
Why spam detection is not phishing detection

Spam is unsolicited bulk messaging, mostly promotional; phishing and scams are deceptive messages aiming at credentials or money. P04 and P05 show these classes are separate and easily confused (P05: all models struggled to separate spam from smishing).
[Reported] P05; [Our reading]
Why English SMS is not Malayalam or Manglish

The corpus is English in Latin script, collected from UK forum posts and volunteer texts. Malayalam script, non-standard romanization (Manglish) and code-mixing change tokenization, spelling variance and vocabulary.
[Reported] P01 data sources; [Our reading]
Source and era confound
Spam came mostly from a forum and ham from volunteer and thesis texts, so a classifier can partly learn source style. The data are from the 2000s, and scam tactics have changed.
B. Most defensible provisional research direction (no F1 target and no fixed dataset size promised)
Directly relevant vs foundational vs indirect

Closest to the task: P08 (pending full text) and P06 (unverified). Language and model foundations: P12 (data context only), P13, P14, P15, plus the baseline P01. Indirect methods and cautions: P02, P03, P04, P05, P07, P09, P10, P11. No paper in the set is a Malayalam or Manglish phishing study.
Survey sheet
Gap supported by the evidence

Within the reviewed set, nothing evaluates phishing or scam detection on Malayalam script, Manglish or Malayalam-English text with documented provenance and leakage-aware splits. This must be stated narrowly, because search snippets show Dravidian SMS spam datasets that include Malayalam. The defensible gap is phishing/scam-specific, form-aware evaluation, not 'first work on Malayalam'.
Gap sheet A and C
What the project can contribute without overstating novelty

(1) A documented labelling protocol and corpus, with each message tagged by form (Malayalam script, Manglish, mixed) and provenance (natural, translated, generated). (2) A controlled comparison of a TF-IDF linear SVM with one multilingual transformer, reported per form with grouped splits. (3) Analysis of spam-vs-scam confusion and of Manglish tokenization.
Is SVM + one multilingual transformer still justified?

Yes as a minimal design. P01 supports a linear SVM as a strong baseline, and P04/P07 show transformer vs classical comparisons are standard. Choose between MuRIL and XLM-R only after a tokenizer diagnostic on a pilot sample, since neither paper shows Manglish phishing results. Also report a trivial baseline, as P01 does.
Datasets actually usable vs contextual

Usable for sanity checks only: UCI SMS Spam (English) and the Mishra-Soni SMS Phishing set (English). Contextual only: DravidianCodeMix (sentiment/offensive labels), Multilingual Spam Data (machine-translated), the proprietary P08 data, PhishNet Dataset2 (synthetic spam). Candidates to verify: SMSDHL and Dravidian Spam SMS (Malayalam spam labels, not phishing).
Dataset Audit
Resolve before collection and training

(a) Exact label definitions for SCAM/PHISHING vs BENIGN, including where promotional spam and OTP or bank notices belong, with written guidelines and an agreement check. (b) Data sources, consent, privacy and PII redaction. (c) A rule for assigning form tags, and a Manglish spelling-variant policy. (d) Benign and scam messages from comparable channels and periods to avoid source shortcuts. (e) Split design grouped by template, campaign and near-duplicate; no augmentation before the split. (f) Per-form metrics with seeds and intervals. (g) Verify P06 and P08 languages and the Dravidian SMS resources.
